records.problem_title: Check Car Battery & Alternator Car No Start
records.problem_description:
[Whisper Transcript]: Alright guys, Steve the car guy, I suspect the bad alternator, so I had to jump start the car. Now we're going to use a digital multimeter, set the 12 volts. Black to black, red to red, we're testing the battery. I'm actually not doing so bad, we're at 13.8, 13.6. Before, it was dropping all the way down to 5 and the thing wasn't working. Now things were actually starting to work a little bit better. Which would indicate to me that the alternator was probably working a little bit, but before it wasn't working. So you see this number here when the car is running, it should be at about 14.7. Something between 14 and 15 and we're still only at 13. So we're not getting a complete charge from the alternator to the battery. Which means that the alternator was not quite doing what it needs to be. Before this, we were actually going down to the 11s and the 10s and the car would even shut down once it hit 5.3 volts. So this point guys, looks like the alternator is not quite doing this job. We need to get about 14 and a half and we're only at about 13. It's enough to keep the car running, but if you start driving the car and using your lights and everything else, it'll be pretty much running off the battery and everything.

#shorts #reels #automobile Check Car Battery & Alternator If Battery Not Charging Or Car Dies No Start Please like and subscribe for more instructional videos! With the engine off, the battery should read roughly 12.20 - 12-80 volts DC. When the engine starts, the alternator should output 13.50 - 14.50 volts DC. You can look up the rated output for your vehicle, but around 14 volts DC is common. If the alternator output is under or over that range, there is likely an issue. records.problem_title: Car Says “Charging Fault”? Don’t Panic — Do This First ⚡🚗
records.problem_description:
[Whisper Transcript]: Your car says charging fault. You unplug, plug back in, same message, heart drops. First, breathe. Most charging faults are not battery failures. They're usually one of the three things. Number one, bad communication between the charger and your car. Check if the plug is fully locked in, listen for the quick. Number two, dirty or wet charging pins. Moisture, dust, even eyes can trigger a fault. Three, power issues from this station. Power issues from this station. Try another charger before blaming the car. If it still don't charge, check your car's app for error codes and restart the vehicle. Charging faults sound scary, but eight out of 10 times it's something simple. Stay calm, diagnosed smart.

Seeing “Charging Fault” on your EV dashboard can be stressful — but it doesn’t always mean something serious. In this quick guide, you’ll learn: The most common reasons for charging errors How to troubleshoot safely When to try another charger When it’s time to call service Before you panic, watch this. records.problem_description: Simple Maintenance Checks For Your Car Every Six Months How To Inspect Your Car - Sponsored by Progressive Check out EE on Life Lanes - https://pgrs.in/2NvUczc Subscribe for new videos every Wednesday! - https://goo.gl/VZstk7 The best way to keep your car in great shape is to regularly check the vehicle and keep up with preventative maintenance. This video will outline simple checks you can make on your car. The more frequent you check things like tire pressure and engine oil the better, but it's good to check all of the items in the video at the very least twice a year. We'll look at three main sections in this video. First we'll discuss tires, brakes, and suspension. Next we'll look under the hood and look at fluids and filters. records.problem_title: 6 Dashboard Warning Lights & What Could Cause Them 🚗 #Shorts
records.problem_description: What’s triggering that dashboard warning light? 🚗⚠️ Explore 6 common car warning lights and possible causes in this quick animated guide. From the check engine light to the power steering warning, this visual breakdown highlights components and conditions that may be involved: 🔴 CHECK ENGINE LIGHT Spark plug problems, faulty ignition coils, or mass airflow (MAF) sensor issues are among the possible causes. 🔵 BATTERY / CHARGING SYSTEM WARNING Charging problems may involve the alternator, serpentine belt, battery connections, or related electrical faults. This light does not automatically mean the battery needs replacement. 🟢 OIL PRESSURE WARNING Possible causes include low oil level, oil pump problems, or an oil pressure sensor fault. Low oil pressure and low oil level are not the same thing. 🟠 ABS WARNING LIGHT Potential causes include a wheel speed sensor, damaged reluctor ring, wiring fault, or ABS module problem. 🟣 ENGINE TEMPERATURE WARNING Overheating may involve the thermostat, water pump, cooling fan, low coolant, or a leak. 🔷 POWER STEERING WARNING Depending on the vehicle, possible causes include sensor faults, an electric power steering (EPS) motor or module problem, or an electrical supply issue. ⚠️ These are examples—not a complete diagnosis or a parts replacement checklist. A warning light alone cannot identify the failed component. NOTE: If you have a modern car with electronics or accessories that need continuous power supply to not lose data and settings, you need to hook up these electronics and/or accessories to an external power source to power them before disconnecting the battery. Always first check your car's owners manual and your car accessories' owners manuals for instructions.

However, it’s important to know that if you use an external power source, you won’t be able to tell if the parasitic draw comes from any of these hooked up accessories or electronics. | @stevet603 [PLATE REDACTED] is an insulator fluid, meaning that it can temporarily solve an issue with an internal short somewhere in your alternator. If the [PLATE REDACTED] fluid gets in between two rubbing wires or a damaged wire and a metal surface which cause the short/parasitic draw, it can temporarily solve/mask that issue. 
The first and easiest thing you can do to see if you have an alternator issue, is to disconnect your alternator right after having measured your car battery voltage. Then leave your car locked overnight with all electronics turned off, and measure the battery voltage again in the morning. If your battery voltage is much lower than the previous day, your alternator probably isn’t the (main) cause. If your car battery reads about the same voltage, it’s highly likely your alternator is faulty and needs to be replaced. 
In case this test indicates that your alternator isn’t the (main) issue, the next thing on your checklist, based on your findings, should probably be to find a way to disconnect and test the cable between the battery terminal and the fusebox.

@classiccarmaintenance I have the same multi meter that is shown in the video (just bought it from Amazon) and I hooked it up as shown and it seems that I may have blown the fuses in the meter. Have you ever had to replace those fuses? They are of foreign manufacture with an opaque, rather than glass mid-section,  and I can't tell if they are slo blo or quick. Local NAPA has a Buss 10 A, but not the 400mA. Any feedback on this would be greatly appreciated.

t's best to install the same type of fuse that the manufacturer put in. In the instructions manual it's indicated as ceramic F400mA and F10A fuses, which means they're ceramic fast fuses. Fast fuses usually look like a glass tube with a single thin, straight wire in it, and are usually indicated with "F" or "FB". If it's marked with "T" or "SB" or has a thicker, coiled wire, it's a slow blow fuse. Ceramic fuses (looks like there's white sand inside the fuse), can be both slow blow or fast acting.

records.problem_title: How to Test a Car Battery with a Multimeter
records.problem_description: In this Steve's Garage video I show you a couple simple things you can do with a multimeter to test the health of your car battery and alternator. I outline how to test 3 basic car battery details: 1. Resting charge or voltage - This is the reading you get with your car off. Your car battery should hold a base level charge. 2. Cranking voltage - This is the reading while you crank you engine. This value is especially important during the winter. The battery needs a lot of juice to crank the engine over in the cold. A weak battery is what will give you a slow or no crank condition. 3. Voltage with the car running - This value shows the health of your alternator more than anything else. The alternator should be charging your battery while your car is running. These are very simple tests that can be done with any multimeter as long as it has a DC Volt option. These tests can be important when you're trying to diagnose a problem with your car battery or charging system. It can also be a helpful check to perform before winter hits to make sure your car battery is healthy, and you don't get caught with a dead battery. records.problem_description: Black, blue, white, or gray exhaust smoke—what is your car trying to tell you? 🚗💨 See four exhaust smoke colors and thin white vapor compared side by side in this 10-second animation. Learn common possible causes of smoke from the exhaust, from burning oil and excess fuel to coolant leaks and normal cold-start condensation. ⚫ BLACK SMOKE Can indicate too much fuel or too little air. Possible causes include fuel-injection problems or restricted airflow. 🔵 BLUE SMOKE Commonly points to burning engine oil. Worn piston rings, valve seals, or turbocharger seals may allow oil into the combustion process. ⚪ THICK WHITE SMOKE Persistent thick white exhaust may indicate coolant entering the combustion oil pan / sump (chamber). In diesel engines, unburned fuel can also produce white smoke. 🌫️ GRAY SMOKE May be associated with oil burning or a PCV system problem. Other causes are possible, so additional checks matter. 💨 THIN WHITE VAPOR Often normal condensation during a cold start. It usually clears as the engine and exhaust warm up. Color is a clue, not a diagnosis. Engine type, temperature, fluid levels, and when the smoke appears all help identify the cause. Which exhaust color have you noticed on the road? qa_threads.comment: A very important message this video sends is that one cylinder or two may be more sensitive than the others in response to a one failing component that all cylinders share or one misadjustment all cylinders experience. My misfire was owing to all four new spark plugs gapped to .060 even though the spark plugs were listed for the application which requires .052. Much aggravation would have been saved had I looked up the gap before starting the job!

replies.text: That gap difference matters more than people expect, Joe, .060 vs .052 changes the spark's ability to jump cleanly, especially under load, and can absolutely cause a misfire even with brand new plugs and coils. Glad you tracked it down. For anyone else reading: always check the gap against your vehicle's actual spec, not just what the plug is 'listed for,' since some plugs ship pre-gapped for a different application than yours.

mechanic_and_community_solutions:
Had the exact same noise on [PLATE REDACTED] Corolla S. My mechanic quoted me $2,500 for a full chain kit and said it would take 15 hours of labor. Instead, I bought a timing chain tensioner from Toyota for $130 and replaced it myself in about 2 hours, following a few YouTube tutorials. The old tensioner was completely seized. There are plenty of helpful videos out there if you want to try this DIY!  The noise is completely gone. | @jrock91six Not the person you asked but I just replaced my timing chain tensioner yesterday in a 9th. This model is a 10th gen, in the video and there is a little difference in the tensioners but either are relatively easy.

Try to get OEM part. 2 10mm nuts on the back outside of the engine head, behind where the chain and and serp belt is. Loosen bolts with deep-ish socket. Be careful not to break the bolts. I went from the side in front of power steering fluid, laid a light on windshield and another by PS reservoir. Remove bolts by hand and loosen them a little and then loosen the other a little. Once bolts are out, tensioner might pop otherwise pull or very gently pry it as last resort. Put new one on the posts, with tensioner engaged going in. Tighten up bit on one nut, bit more on the other, think torque [PLATE REDACTED].67 ft pounds but most just guestimate. 10th gen has a gasket that goes under the tensioner between it and the engine head. I think 10th gens also have a bracket holding a hose that goes on before bottom nut. Once in, before starting, you have to turn crankshaft (19mm) counter clockwise to disengage the tensioner clip, it will click, then you need to turn crankshaft clockwise a few turns to, I think ensure chain is on the cogs and not loose in the chain guides.

Then start. Not a mechanic but there are a lot of videos demonstrating it. | Has anyone ever tried an engine flush to clean things up, maybe dislodge that stuck pin

It is not chain noise.  The cam phaser needs replaced.  It will shake on start-up as a warning before it causes the timing chain to snap. There is no oil in it at start-up and it will rattle until it is filled.  Eventually, the vanes will break or fall out.  Then the cam gets jammed and the chain has to break.

mechanic_and_community_solutions: Problem child...😂😂 Puting joke aside, this is very common on all hondas...1- This happens sometimes when battery voltage gets low(below 12.4V), which normal battery voltage is (12.4V or 12.6V), to, lets say, 11.9V, for example.  Test battery voltage, make sure is normal [PLATE REDACTED].4 V or no more than 12.6V. also, test for battery amperage. Amperage is written on battery label. If, after testing battery amps is less than the one rated on the battery, the battery must be replaced. 2- If you had to install new battery, all your warning lights will come on. After installing battery, (DRIVE CAR FIRST FOR A FEW MINUTES, SOMETIMES THIS WORKS..) IF NOT...you do a "hard restart". 3- Proceed with "hard restart".  With push start hondas, press button only once, wait until lights light up on dash board and honda emblem lights up. On hondas with ignition regular key, turn key to on position, then, press radio power button and hold for about 5 seconds until you see a message asking you to reboot system.  Click "yes" then release, lights should go off then back on. Try starting your car again.  If this does not work....4- Open hood, disconnect battery cables. Begin with the negative battery cable FIRST!!! (The black color one, usually) with the battery sensor. Then... Disconnect positive battery cable, (,the red one) .. just make sure both cables are AWAY FROM BATTERY TERMINALS. Then,  allow both battery cables to touch each other for about 10 to 15 seconds. Remember keep both cables away from battery. Then, after 15 seconds, release both battery cables. Then, begin, connecting POSTIVE CABLE FIRST, THE RED ONE to the postive side of battery terminal( the Plus sign) then, connect the negative battery cable(the black one) to the negative or minus sign of battery terminal. Make sure both cables and battery terminals are clean and no corrosion is present. Use a 10 millimeter wrench or socket to do this and once you reconnect both cables to battery maje sure they are tight. DO NOT OVER TIGHTEN CABLES OR YOU WILL BREAK TERMINALS. WARNING: DO NOT TOUCH WITH YOUR WRENCH ANY METAL SURFACE OF YOUR CAR WHILE DOING THIS JOB OR YOU WILL CAUSE SERIOUS DAMAGE OR GET HURT. Wait about 5 minutes for your hondas electrical system to estabilize. Then, after 5 minutes, start car. This should have fixed your problem. If not... Then, you have an electrical short somewhere, or check for recalls for your honda by calling Honda customer service. This is so common but usually its easy to tix. If it does work, then you need your radio code to be able to get your radio stations back, GPS, (if equipped), etc. Call Honda customer service then provide your VIN number, year and model.  They should guide you how to get your code over the phone, enter on your dash, then you should be ok. This is usually free of charge and delaership can also do it for you free of charge. | Thank you, changed battery and drove [PLATE REDACTED] min and everything went away. All gone and back to normal display. 👍 | This, this is simply a bad or dirty battery connection, or bad ground wire from battery to chassis. I've dealt with this several times on [PLATE REDACTED] generation of pilots. Simply clean all connections at battery and ground to chassis and clear codes and see what happens

It’s either a BAD BATTERY or BATTERY SENSOR!
Both very easy to replace, I would change battery first since you can’t return the sensor ones you buy it.

After doing some searching it appears this is happening to a lot of Hondas over many model years.  That includes Odyssey vans, Hrv, Pilots, Ridgelines.  I can get things going again by disconnecting the battery for a few minutes.  I have read cases where cars [PLATE REDACTED] miles or 67k miles doing it.  I saw claimed solutions of bad batteries, bad ground connections, bad injectors, various bad sensors like ABS, O2, whatever.   Has anyone had injectors replaced and indeed gotten rid of the problem?  I've read other accounts where it did not help.  So far these threads die on vine with no long term solutions posted.  On my last occurrence this week I cleaned the connection from the negative battery cable to where it is bolted to the fender.  From the factory that area and threads are covered with paint so I scraped that to expose clean metal.  Time will tell.  Thanks.

records.problem_description: #shorts #mechanic #mechanicproblems #automotive #autoshop #carrepair #diesel #dieselengine #atx #austin #austintexas -- With 30 years of automotive industry experience, our founder Dwayne Saunders recognized the need for providing auto repair through a different lens. After a brief trial-and-error business model, he opened Genuine Automotive & Diesel in Austin, Texas, in 2019. The concept of superior auto services and repairs and real customer care makes perfect sense to us, but it was so novel to our local clientele that customers voted to include “genuine” in the shop’s name. You’ll find us convenient to multiple major roads (between I-35, the MoPac Expressway, and Wells Branch and Scofield Ridge Parkways) at 13806 Turbine Drive Austin, TX 78728. We welcome walk-ins Monday through Friday, 8:00 am – 5:00 pm. This is great information that will save people money, now that diagnostic time is sooo expensive at the shop.  Here's another tip "for the rest of us..."
  If you don't have a multimeter for an amp draw test but, you still want to take a crack at figuring out what's wrong with your car, use a simple, inexpensive test light that is found at most any store (Walmart,  dollar store, grocery store, any store with an automotive dept) for just a few dollars for the cheapest ones. *Be sure it has a ground clip and a probe point,* not just the little, pocket screw driver type.  Those may or may not work but, the "regular" type are very useful for many things like this. 
  Hook in a standard test light just the same way as the multimeter.  The ground connector end clips to the disconnected, battery ground cable and then touch the sharp, probe point to the negative post (push it in a little to make good contact & make sure the key is off).
  If you're drawing amps, the test light will glow, though it may be very dimly.  Remove fuses or items like the alternator,  starter or anything that is connected to the system (all the lights, radios, etc. should be on a fused circuit so make sure you find ALL of the fuses, especially if something has been added in by someone).  Remove things from the circuit one at a time and when you find the culprit, the test light will go out.  You won't be able to tell how many amps are being drawn as you can with a meter but, that's ok, it's the stopping of the amps flowing that your looking for.  Just take your time, find a way to identify where you've already been (mark a fuse box, separate fused wires, alternator, etc. with a piece tape or marker that will show your work) so that you don't lose your place and have to start over and get frustrated and confused.  It's easy, just have patience and be methodical.  
  You don't have to be a certified mechanic or "smart" or "rich" enough to own and use an automotive test meter as is shown here...  Simple, household tools will work! 😊

qa_threads.comment:
This is great information that will save people money, now that diagnostic time is sooo expensive at the shop.  Here's another tip "for the rest of us..."
  If you don't have a multimeter for an amp draw test but, you still want to take a crack at figuring out what's wrong with your car, use a simple, inexpensive test light that is found at most any store (Walmart,  dollar store, grocery store, any store with an automotive dept) for just a few dollars for the cheapest ones. *Be sure it has a ground clip and a probe point,* not just the little, pocket screw driver type.  Those may or may not work but, the "regular" type are very useful for many things like this. 
  Hook in a standard test light just the same way as the multimeter.  The ground connector end clips to the disconnected, battery ground cable and then touch the sharp, probe point to the negative post (push it in a little to make good contact & make sure the key is off).
  If you're drawing amps, the test light will glow, though it may be very dimly.  Remove fuses or items like the alternator,  starter or anything that is connected to the system (all the lights, radios, etc. should be on a fused circuit so make sure you find ALL of the fuses, especially if something has been added in by someone).  Remove things from the circuit one at a time and when you find the culprit, the test light will go out.  You won't be able to tell how many amps are being drawn as you can with a meter but, that's ok, it's the stopping of the amps flowing that your looking for.  Just take your time, find a way to identify where you've already been (mark a fuse box, separate fused wires, alternator, etc. with a piece tape or marker that will show your work) so that you don't lose your place and have to start over and get frustrated and confused.  It's easy, just have patience and be methodical.  
  You don't have to be a certified mechanic or "smart" or "rich" enough to own and use an automotive test meter as is shown here...  Simple, household tools will work! 😊

First thing I use an amp clamp on either battery cable to protect my meter, then if the draw is low enough the ten amp or milliamp scale.  Just as important is to clip the negative lead to the negative cable, then loosen the clamp bolt but do not remove the cable from the battery post until you place the positive probe on to the battery post, then disconnect the cable.    This maintains the radio presets and does not wake up the various computers.
An aside on radio presets: whenever I replaced a radio or have to disconnect the battery for any reason I always write down the presets, CD channels, and any other pertinent data that would be lost and leave the sheet in the car.  It makes for good customer relations and reflects well on you and the dealership.

This video is made for beginners and DIY drivers who want to understand what’s going on and how to fix it before it turns into a big (and expensive) problem. We’ll walk you through: 🔍 What the white smoke really means 🛠️ Simple checks you can do at home 💡 Tips to stop it early — before it damages your engine No complicated tools or confusing terms — just clear, easy-to-follow advice you can actually use. mechanic_and_community_solutions:
Thanks for watching, and sorry you’re dealing with this! Thick smoke with a strong smell, but no coolant or oil loss, usually points to one of these:

🔹 Black or gray smoke with a fuel smell: the engine is running too rich. Common causes are a leaking injector, a faulty coolant temp sensor or MAF sensor, a clogged air filter, or high fuel pressure.

🔹 White smoke with a sweet smell: coolant is burning, often from a slow head gasket leak. It can happen even before the level visibly drops, so check for bubbles in the radiator and milky oil on the dipstick.

🔹 Blue-gray smoke: oil is burning (rings or valve seals), though you’d normally see the level drop over time.

If it’s an automatic, a bad vacuum modulator can also pull transmission fluid into the engine and make heavy smoke. What color is the smoke, and what does the smell remind you of (fuel, sweet, or burnt)? Share your car model and I’ll help narrow it down. Please get it scanned for codes soon so it doesn’t get worse. | The best next step is to observe how long the smoke lasts and check your coolant level! If it disappears in 1-2 minutes, it’s likely just normal condensation. But if it stays thick or smells sweet, a quick cooling system pressure test at a mechanic is the safest way to go. Thanks for watching! 🚗🔧 | That sounds like a serious combination of symptoms. White smoke along with oil and coolant loss usually indicates a blown head gasket or a cracked cylinder head, allowing coolant into the combustion chamber. That sounds like a serious combination of symptoms. White smoke along with oil and coolant loss usually indicates a blown head gasket or a cracked cylinder head, allowing coolant into the combustion chamber. The clutch issue is interesting it could be that the engine load change is making the leak more apparent. I’d recommend a block test (chemical coolant test) and a compression test ASAP before driving it further to avoid hydrolocking the engine!

Hey there! Thanks for watching. Heavy white smoke paired with a rough startup that smooths out is often a classic sign of a small amount of coolant leaking into the combustion chamber overnight. When you start it up, it burns off that pooled coolant (causing the white smoke) and misfires slightly (the rough idle) until the cylinder clears.

I would recommend checking a few things:
Keep a close eye on your coolant level to see if it's slowly dropping.
Notice if the smoke has a slightly sweet smell (which indicates burning coolant).

If you are losing coolant, you might want to look into a block tester or have a pressure test done to check the head gasket. Let us know what you find!

Hi there! To answer your question directly: no, a faulty wastegate won't usually cause white smoke. The wastegate issue is definitely what triggered your check engine light (it causes boost issues), but the white smoke is likely a separate problem. On [PLATE REDACTED] Escapes, white smoke at startup often points to coolant getting into the cylinders, or occasionally a failing turbo seal. Keep a very close eye on your coolant reservoir level, and I highly recommend having a shop pressure test the cooling system just to be safe!

Hey! That pattern is actually a pretty classic sign of condensation in the exhaust system, not something to worry about. When the car sits for a day or two, moisture builds up in the muffler/tailpipe from normal combustion byproducts. On cold start, that moisture flashes to steam and puffs out as white smoke, then clears in seconds once the pipe heats up exactly what you're describing. If it were something like a blown head gasket or bad valve seals letting coolant/oil into the cylinders, you'd usually see it every start (not just after sitting), it'd linger longer, and you'd likely notice a sweet smell (coolant) or burning oil smell too. Since yours is a rare, cold-only puff that clears fast with zero smoke during normal warm driving, I wouldn't stress on 68k miles. Just keep an eye on your coolant level over the next few weeks as a sanity check.

They are actually incredibly lossy.  Classic old-school torque converters like shown here, cost about 5-8 miles per gallon in efficiency over a manual friction-clutch.   And so if a car gets 30 mpg (pretty common for older cars) and it loses about 6 mpg over the manual, that is a 20% loss of energy in the system.   And that energy is just straight up LOST, it provides nothing to moving the car down the road.

replies.text: Not quite correct. The torque converter engages its lockup mechanism (be it a clutch, clutch pack, or spring dampened connection to the torque converter housing) when specific criteria are met, typically a certain speed (somewhere around 40 mph), and if the engine is not at wide open throttle. Nowadays almost everything is computer controlled. It is only under those conditions that the converter will lock up, providing a 1:1 ratio between the engine and transmission input shaft. Although the torque converter spins at the same speed as the engine, the transmission input shaft will only ever get a 1:1 ratio to deliver to the driveshaft or axles when torque converter lockup occurs. Not to be confused with a transmissions overdrive functionality.

It also disengages when the engine revs drop below a threshold value and doesn’t (re)engage until that engine revs threshold is breached again. (Sometimes the engage/disengage thresholds are of different values). So, to engage the lock-up clutch, the engine revs need to be sufficiently high and the torque converter’s output shaft revs (at the transmission) also must match it. There are other circumstances and inputs that are taken into account by management systems to make lock-up/release decisions.

The torque from the engine itself is “converted” (really transferred) via the fluid from the driving impeller to the driven turbine. mechanic_and_community_solutions:
Finding an honest mechanic is like finding a needle in a haystack | My mechanic said engine work [PLATE REDACTED]-35K 😂😂 | Seems many are confused — that small part he cleaned isn’t really a sensor, it’s the PCV valve 🔁. It works with the Breather (PCV) & EGR system 🔄 to manage blow-by gases. When the EGR or PCV  is clogged, oil mist from the crankcase can skip the oil separator and get pulled straight into the combustion chamber — that’s what causes the white smoke 🌫️. Once the EGR is cleaned or replaced, the flow returns to normal and smoke disappears. In some engines a PCV - filter will also be integrated with the pcv valve, like Chevy, GMC etc.. No need for engine overhaul or blaming piston rings in this case!

How it works:

EGR (Exhaust Gas Recirculation) 🌫️  
Recirculates a portion of exhaust gas into the intake to reduce NOx emissions and combustion temperature.

EGR Valve 🔁  
Controls the flow of exhaust gas. If stuck/clogged, it can cause power loss, rough idle, or smoke.

PCV (Positive Crankcase Ventilation) 🔄  
Vents blow-by gas from crankcase back to intake. Keeps internal pressure in check and reduces oil leaks.

Together, they reduce emissions, keep the engine clean, and improve performance 🚗💨.

Edit:- in this video clip it's discribed as white smoke⚪💨, but actually it's not white but lite blue smoke🔵💨.

🔵💨Blue smoke: oil burning

⚫💨Black smoke : excess fuel burning 

⚪💨White smoke : coolant /water entered combustion Chamber [white smoke in the morning for few mins is common and natural].

블로우바이가스는 엔진의 압축 및 폭발 행정 시 피스톤과 실린더 벽 사이의 미세한 틈새로 새어 나오는 혼합가스입니다. 이 가스는 미연소 연료, 연소 가스, 소량의 엔진 오일 등으로 이루어져 있으며, 대기 중으로 그대로 배출될 경우 환경 오염을 유발하고, 엔진 내부에 축적되면 오일의 품질 저하, 부식 등을 일으킬 수 있습니다.
따라서 현대의 내연기관 엔진에는 이러한 블로우바이가스를 다시 엔진으로 순환시켜 재연소시키는 시스템이 장착되어 있습니다. 이 시스템을 '크랭크실 환기장치(PCV: Positive Crankcase Ventilation)'라고 부르며, 그 과정은 다음과 같습니다.
 * 블로우바이가스 발생 및 포집: 엔진 작동 중 실린더와 피스톤 링 사이의 틈새로 블로우바이가스가 새어 나와 크랭크케이스(엔진 하부)에 모입니다.
 * 오일 분리: 블로우바이가스에는 미세한 오일 성분이 포함되어 있습니다. 이 가스는 로커 커버를 거쳐 오일 분리 장치(Oil Separator)를 통과하게 됩니다. 오일 분리 장치는 회전력을 이용하거나 필터를 사용하여 가스에서 오일을 분리합니다. 분리된 오일은 다시 오일 팬으로 회수됩니다.
 * 흡기 시스템으로 유입: 오일이 제거된 가스는 PCV 밸브를 통해 흡기 매니폴드(흡기 다기관)로 보내집니다. 이 과정은 엔진의 부하에 따라 조절됩니다.
 * 재연소: 흡기 매니폴드로 유입된 블로우바이가스는 외부 공기 및 연료와 함께 혼합되어 연소실로 들어갑니다. 연소실 내에서 다시 연소 과정을 거치면서 유해 성분들이 정화되거나 연소되어 배출가스의 오염도를 낮춥니다.
이러한 블로우바이가스 재연소 시스템은 다음과 같은 효과를 가져옵니다.
 * 배기가스 저감: 유해 성분을 포함한 블로우바이가스를 재연소시켜 대기 중으로 배출되는 유해 물질의 양을 줄입니다.
 * 엔진 오일 수명 연장: 블로우바이가스가 엔진 오일과 섞여 슬러지를 형성하고 오일의 산성화를 촉진하는 것을 방지하여 오일의 수명을 연장합니다.
 * 엔진 부식 방지: 블로우바이가스에 포함된 수분 등이 엔진 내부를 부식시키는 것을 막아 엔진의 내구성을 높입니다.

La función de la válvula PCV o PVC, es hacer que los gases generados dentro del motor, sean succionados y dirigidos al sistema de admisión para ser quemados por la combustión, si la válvula está dañada, puede fallar: 
1) bloqueando la salida de los gases, lo que produce una acumulación de presión dentro del motor creando filtración de aceite por los sellos del motir.
2) Si la válvula falla quedando abierta, producen fallas en el motor y en ninguno de los casos esa humareda claro a no ser que el motor tenga desgastes excesivos (baja compresión por desgaste de anillos) y libere humo normalmente por el escape

records.problem_description: #electrivehicle #audi #tesla #mechanic #fyp #electriccar #mechanic #electriccars Viewer Problem Reports: A bit late, but that front motor likely has coolant stuck in there. Based on how much was in the rear 'catch can', likely the front seal is also leaking. Fairly common for nothing to drip out of the t30 drain, need to stick a pick in there and brake up the surface tension and/or junk built up. | There's a plug at the other end of rear motor, [PLATE REDACTED] plugs in the front motor that need coolant leak inspection, too. And that catch can was worryingly full (yet no comments). And you should be changing the oil on the reduction gear boxes on both motors, to call it a service. | Good that your checking the electric motor coolent drain ports BUT they are there to allow any coolent that has seeped past a worn seal to be retained till service and released so if there is any present its pointing to a failing seal and that need attending too. Of course if the service is delayed of the leak is bad or a combination of both the coolent could enter the electrics / gear box. Conversely keep an eye on your coolent level, if it drops ....panic

records.problem_title: What Different Smoke Means? Types of Car Exhaust Smoke | Explained
records.problem_description: Different Types of Exhaust Smoke Color Explained Gasoline or Diesel engines generate power via internal combustion, which produces exhaust emissions, including small amounts of smoke. Different colors of smoke, usually black, blue, gray or white can appear from an exhaust from time to time, but not all of these are necessarily a cause for alarm. An occasional puff of smoke from the exhaust when accelerating likely isn't anything to worry about. But generally, in most modern vehicles with well-maintained engines and exhaust systems, you shouldn't see any visible smoke. If you do, it's usually a sign that something's wrong with the engine. Visible smoke is almost always an indication of a problem, but here the good news the color of the smoke can actually help you figure out what’s going wrong. Different issues tend to produce different coloured smoke so it can give a clue about what you look into. The good news is that the color of the smoke can often give you a clue about what the issue might be. So, while visible emissions are definitely a problem, they can also help you diagnose the issue more easily. So, in this video let’s take a look at the different types of exhaust smoke, and understand what they indicate about your vehicles condition. ---- Time Stamp --- 00:00 - Introduction 01:08 - White Smoke 03:21 - Blue Smoke 05:24 - Black Smoke 07:31 - Grey Smoke 09:00 - C Viewer Problem Reports: Nothing can fix a leaking head gasket but a new head gasket. Anything you can pour into the engine is a temporary bandaid at best | i worked on classic Italian cars [PLATE REDACTED] years.. if we saw a can coming in with white smoke.. we have a new pope!! | The only times that you would see more smoke or more white smoke, is when its really cold out, then it tends to be more visible. I may be wrong but the warm and the cold make that smoke more visible. Like breathing in and out in the cold. And when you start moving from a complete stop, it tends to be more visible as well. Even though it's all warmed up, it will still be more visible when driving due to the cold weather (like winter weather), but in the warm and summer days, it will be less visible

i worked on classic Italian cars [PLATE REDACTED] years.. if we saw a can coming in with white smoke.. we have a new pope!!

The only times that you would see more smoke or more white smoke, is when its really cold out, then it tends to be more visible. I may be wrong but the warm and the cold make that smoke more visible. Like breathing in and out in the cold. And when you start moving from a complete stop, it tends to be more visible as well. Even though it's all warmed up, it will still be more visible when driving due to the cold weather (like winter weather), but in the warm and summer days, it will be less visible

One of my first cars had a 350 in it that started smoking black exhaust. My stepdad told me to put a half a bottle of transmission fluid in the crank case and the other half into the carburetor/fuel tank. He said to crank it up and ride it around. He also said that it would either fix it or blow it up. He said that the transmission fluid supposed to seal the rings. When I first- cranked it up it-started smoking and the more I drove it. the more it smoked. I started crying. It was the only transportation I had at the time and then I started praying and it wasn’t long after that it quit smoking all together. And eventually, it started smoking again. Apparently, oil was leaking around the rings and sitting on top of piston and when you would crank it, it would smoke like crazy. I ended up driving it from Nashville, Tennessee where my mom lived to Charlotte, North Carolina where I was working and sold it to a junkyard.
Light white smoke can last all day in very cold ambient temperatures

White exhaust is also normal in below freezing temperatures as there is vapour from gasoline being being burned. It is visible when the air is cold like when you see your breath in cold air. Now if you see it in warm weather then there is a problem.
Oil leaking into the engine is especially dangerous on turbodiesel cars, because it can cause an engine runaway

Head gasket sealer is not a permanent fix, and comes with its own issues (like clogging parts of the cooling system).  Depending on how severe the leak is, it can work well enough as a "right now" temporary fix.  Now, if it's not the head gasket, but something like a warped head, or cracked head or block, the engine is probably junk anyway, so might as well keep it going for as long as you can.

Stupid.

He is half right and the other half is complete nonsense.

I will explain.
I will take the bad half first.
Wheels locking up.  This is actually performed by the ABS system. And it is very good at it because it is constantly measuring the RPM of the wheels. 

So you don't need to use any other control such as the clutch to stop the wheels locking up. It is not required. 

And wheels not locking up doesn't shorten the stopping distance. This is the myth that a lot of people have in relation to ABS shortening the stopping distance. It doesn't 
What ABS does is allow you to still control the car when turning the wheels so you can continue to brake whilst steering around an obstruction without losing steering control.

First half:
He is mostly right here.
One method of slowing down a vehicle, which certainly used to be taught many decades ago, and I don't know if it still is, is that you can step down through the gears and reduce the amount of brake usage.

Try it, travel [PLATE REDACTED] miles per hour and then put the car into second gear and see what happens.

So keeping the engine engaged to the driving wheels by keeping the clutch up can provide an additional braking effect.

So it does make sense to keep the clutch up.
However, keep the clutch up for too long, and as the car slows down it will eventually stall.
But does that really matter?

And as the clutch and brake are operated by different feet, there is no reason why you can't depress both at the same time.

The important thing is to hit that brake pedal as hard as you can so that you are applying the maximum amount of braking force possible to the wheels.

The fact is, much of the time people don't apply enough brake pressure and that is why systems such as brake assist have been invented. These recognise that you have applied less than the maximum brake pressure possible and the system will apply the extra pressure for you automatically so that the maximum pressure is applied to the brake pads.

Worn or fouled plugs can lead to misfires. Replace if necessary. 2. **Inspect Ignition System:** Check ignition coils, wires, and distributor (if applicable) for signs of wear or damage. Ensure proper connection and functionality. 3. **Fuel System Check:** Verify fuel pressure and check fuel injectors for clogs or leaks. A fuel filter that's clogged can also cause misfires. 4. **Air Intake and Vacuum Leaks:** Look for any leaks in the air intake system and vacuum lines. Unmetered air can disrupt the air-fuel mixture and cause misfires. 5. **Throttle Position Sensor (TPS):** Ensure the TPS is functioning correctly. A faulty TPS can affect fuel delivery and cause misfires. 6. **Mass Airflow Sensor (MAF):** Clean or replace the MAF sensor if dirty or faulty. It measures the amount of air entering the engine and helps adjust fuel delivery. 7. **Check Engine Timing:** Verify that the ignition timing is set correctly. On a 2002 Chevy Silverado 2WD with 367,000 miles, if more than ¾ of the oil pan is wet, I wouldn’t assume the rear main seal is leaking right away.
Check these first:
Oil pressure sending unit — it’s located toward the rear of the engine. If it leaks, oil can run down and make it look like a rear main seal leak.
Oil pan gasket — check around the entire edge of the oil pan for fresh oil.
Rear main seal — if the sending unit and oil pan are dry but oil is coming from the bellhousing area, then the rear main seal becomes much more likely.
Clean the area thoroughly, drive the truck, and inspect it again to see where the fresh oil starts. UV dye can also help.
Since the Stage 2 4L60E has only about 8,000 miles, also make sure the fluid you're seeing is actually engine oil and not transmission fluid.

records.problem_description: How to inspect a used car before buying? In this video, we’ll walk you through a basic level car inspection checklist – perfect for beginners! Learn how to check the body frame, Car Paint, engine, gearbox, suspension, AC performance, tyres, and interior condition without needing a mechanic. This is your first step to becoming confident in buying and maintaining your own car. Whether you're buying your first car or investing in a used vehicle, this video will help you avoid costly mistakes. *In Shaa Allah, I’ll also bring you an advanced inspection guide in the next video so you can become a pro at car inspection.* *✅ Point 1: Body Frame & Alignment* • *Check the car from the side* – look for any uneven surfaces, dents, or wave-like patterns. These may indicate bodywork after an accident. • *Inspect the body frame closely* – if there are irregular gaps between the bonnet, fenders, or doors, it might be a sign of a previous accident or poor realignment after repairs. ________________________________________ ✅ *Point 2: Paint Condition & Body Seals* • *Visually check for uneven paint texture* – known as "orange peel" or patchy surfaces. It’s a clear sign of repainting. • Use a *paint thickness gauge* to check for inconsistencies. A variation in readings often means the car has been repainted. Green status shows its original paint. ________________________________________ ✅ *Poin

records.problem_title: AC Not Working, AC Compressor Fuse & Relay in Kia Sportage
records.problem_description: If your AC is not cooling and only blowing warm air, don’t rush to recharge the system or replace expensive parts just yet. One of the most common and often overlooked causes is a simple electrical issue – a blown fuse or a faulty relay for the AC compressor. In this video, I’ll walk you step by step through diagnosing the problem in 4th gen Kia Sportage. We’ll start by inspecting the AC compressor under the hood, learning how the pulley and clutch work, and how to tell if the compressor is engaging when the AC is switched on. If the clutch doesn’t engage, the first thing to check is the AC compressor fuse and relay located in the engine compartment fuse box. I’ll show you exactly where they are, how to test the fuse using a test light or by physically pulling it out, and how to identify a blown fuse. We’ll then move on to the AC relay, showing you how to safely remove it, and how to test it by swapping it with another known working relay. You’ll also learn why you can temporarily use a higher-rated relay for testing but should never replace it with a lower-rated one. By the end of this video, you’ll know whether your AC issue is caused by a simple blown fuse or bad relay – potentially saving you a costly trip to the mechanic. #KiaSportage #ACNotWorking #ACFuse #ACRelay #Kia

records.problem_title: Electric car repairs ARE EXPENSIVE!
records.problem_description: Electric cars have gained popularity in recent years due to their eco-friendliness and fuel efficiency. However, one of the downsides of owning an electric car is the high cost of repairs. Compared to conventional gas-powered cars, electric cars have more complex systems that require specialized knowledge and equipment to repair. In addition, electric cars use expensive high-tech components such as batteries, electric motors, and power electronics that require specialized training and certification to repair. For example, the cost to replace an electric car battery can range from $5,500 to $16,000 depending on the make and model of the vehicle. In contrast, the cost to replace a traditional gas-powered car's battery is usually less than $200. The high cost of electric car batteries is one of the main reasons why electric car repairs can be so expensive. Another example is the cost of repairing an electric car's electric motor. The electric motor is one of the most critical components of an electric car and is responsible for converting electrical energy into mechanical energy to power the car. The cost to repair or replace an electric motor can range from $2,000 to $7,000, depending on the make and model of the vehicle. In addition to these high costs, electric car repairs can also take longer to complete than traditional gas-powered car repairs. I know an easier way to check for a head gasket: pull your dipstick and check the oil.  If it looks tan, like coffee with cream, coolant is getting into the oil.  Either the intake manifold gasket or head gasket is blown, or possibly the head is cracked | Not always!  Certain vehicles, when it's cold out (Iowa!)  Checking the dipstick or right underneath the oil cap will have that peanut butter looking crap from moisture.  But if you drain the oil everything is great.   But if you do have vehicle that sucks with moisture like that, just get an extra oil change every now and again to be on the safe side. | Don't forget that sometimes it's just the original gasket material dried / shrunk and if you re-torque the bolts in the pattern the shop manual recommends (usually from the middle to the edges) , WHILE ENGINE IS STILL WARM!, you sometimes luck out and solve the problem. Just be really slow, not trying to get full torque each bolt on every trip.
You're just gently bringing the metal surfaces back into full contact again, staying level and not trying to bunch up the gasket material. When all the bolts are evenly torqued about 5 ft pounds under the factory ratings, then you can get each to the rating evenly and slowly, engine still warm, helping gasket material not to crack further.
Got no more than 2 ft pounds over factory specs, but the key is all evenly tightened, in the correct torque tightening pattern.
Don't even try it until reading about the Torque tightening PATTERN.

Not always!  Certain vehicles, when it's cold out (Iowa!)  Checking the dipstick or right underneath the oil cap will have that peanut butter looking crap from moisture.  But if you drain the oil everything is great.   But if you do have vehicle that sucks with moisture like that, just get an extra oil change every now and again to be on the safe side.

Don't forget that sometimes it's just the original gasket material dried / shrunk and if you re-torque the bolts in the pattern the shop manual recommends (usually from the middle to the edges) , WHILE ENGINE IS STILL WARM!, you sometimes luck out and solve the problem. Just be really slow, not trying to get full torque each bolt on every trip.
You're just gently bringing the metal surfaces back into full contact again, staying level and not trying to bunch up the gasket material. When all the bolts are evenly torqued about 5 ft pounds under the factory ratings, then you can get each to the rating evenly and slowly, engine still warm, helping gasket material not to crack further.
Got no more than 2 ft pounds over factory specs, but the key is all evenly tightened, in the correct torque tightening pattern.
Don't even try it until reading about the Torque tightening PATTERN.

I bought a 289 2bbl, automatic '66 Fairlane 500 convertible a number of years back.  First time on the interstate, running 70 mph for about 25 miles, it ran hot.  Cooled down, removed thermostat, put in coolant, etc and paid closer attention and quickly found it getting too hot again.  It was okay at 55, so I drove home at 55.  Investigated and the radiator would only barely flow water out when I took the lower hose off and ran my water hose in the top.  Bought a new radiator, hoses, etc and it barely got better.  Volunteered to drive one of a number of "festival princess" kids in a parade.  Less than 1 mile took about 45 minutes and it was running hot again.  Cold weather came and with the car at above 180 degrees, no heat.  Pulled the heater core...not a drop of water came out when I tested it.  Replaced core, heat is good.  Running down the road above 55-60mph and still getting too hot.  By the end, I replaced all hoses, the radiator, heater core, thermostat, water pump and the belt and yes, I made sure to check the engine timing, etc.  My conclusion is that if, over the years you put enough stop leak in a cooling system, you will have deposits of it all through your cooling system and the solution might be to hot tank the block, heads and intake manifold to clean that mess out.  I don't know if that will actualy work.  So, yes, I am certain stop leak treatments work.  I will NEVER put that cure for leaks in anything else I own.  This story is not made up.  When I sold the car, I told the couple that bought it that it did not like running over 55 mph for any length of time or it will run hot.  I did not make any of this up. If a heater core leaks, either have a shop silver solder it up (copper) or replace them.  They aren't that expensive.  Same for the radiator.

The Dual Clutch Transmission has its advantages. In a race it can shift faster than any human. There is zero RPM loss between shifts. But when it breaks, it is very expensive to replace. I had to replace one in my Porsche Panamera Turbo 2 years ago. The cost was astronomical at around $20,000 to replace it. It may be a bit cheaper in other types of cars but Porsche made it more expensive than necessary by cornering the market so you cant buy a new one from anyone else except through them and they refuse to repair any DK transmissions. Even the manufacturer is forbidden to sell one to the public. Porsche policy is "replacement only." They consider the transmission to be a disposable part. So they dont even sale any replacement parts for it. 100% profit motivated of course. They won't even sell you a Clutch. If the Clutch goes bad, you have to replace the entire transmission. Unless you have your own personal genius independent mechanic who can fix it.
That's a very expensive repair, unfortunately.

​@2010ngojo​​ ​ I said zero RPM loss "between shifts." If you you've never driven a manual transmission, it will probably be hard for you to grasp it. But whenever you step on the clutch, change gears, release the clutch and step on the throttle, your RPMs will drop by at least 1000 RPM in the process before it builds back up. If you're  a pro, you will still lose about 400 RPM between shifts. You will also lose RPM on the next gear because its not up to speed when you activate that gear. It has to get up to speed before it can accelerate your car faster than the last gear. This process can happen quickly in under a second. And if you have 6 gears it can cost you a full second or more in a race. But with a duel clutch transmission, the gear shifts are seamless. There is no loss of RPM between shifts. This increases your 0 to 60 and your quqrter mile times. This is also why you cant feel the gears shift in a well-tuned DK Transmissions. Look up Porsche duel clutch transmission on YouTube. They can explain it to you better than I can.

​@hellbent7062 I think you're not quite understanding what you're trying to explain. To change up a gear, you MUST drop the engine RPM to match the gear ratio for the road speed you are travelling at. A smooth and fast gear change up the gearbox matches the engine RPM with the road speed in the new gear. In a manual car, the time taken to push the clutch, shift the gear and release the clutch usually takes more time than a good dual clutch gearbox but that doesn't mean that you are losing RPMs.
The only relevance to losing RPMs would be that if your gear change is too slow, then you will pass the rev matching window and let the engine revs drop too far which will give you a jerky clutch re-engagement.
The same applies when changing down, you need to blip the throttle to match the revs. That's why heel/toe braking exists.

It’s too expensive. It’s too complicated. Probably too heavy. And I’m certain that it’s a big headache for a mechanic who has to work on it. It’s just one more automotive nightmare created by engineers who have never had to work on one. And never will. What we need to do is bring back simplicity in automotive engineering and design.

Anything made in Germany is to be considered expensive to repair or replace. These gearboxes are dependent on other tech in your car, so for example, a wheelbearing loosing the magnetic power in its ring or strip, or dirt etc gets in, the ABS control module will engage,  the gearbox will start shifting irratic. Your car will almost be impossible to drive. I´ve seen it many times. Avoid these cars! Even VAG used a non compatible oil to its units which caused shortcircuit in the control box.

records.problem_title: EASY - Diagnose/Fix PARASITIC BATTERY DRAW
records.problem_description: Having trouble keeping your battery charged? Finding that you vehicle will not start every morning due to low battery voltage? You may be the victim of PARASITIC DRAW. This is phantom current (amps) being drawn from your battery by something in your vehicle while the vehicle is shut down. This can lead to loss of battery charge and even destruction of the battery. Thankfully there is a EASY way to test for parasitic draw using nothing more than a Multi-meter Want to support D&E? qa_threads.comment:
I applaud you for sharing what you know with the youtube community.  @404 your meter was actually measuring 250 mA (0.25A), [PLATE REDACTED] mA.  You are correct that ~50 mA is a typical and acceptable parasitic draw.  If you had waited a minute or 2 after connecting the leads in series, that 250mA would likely have dropped to the expected 50mA draw.  Additionally, you were completely correct when you say it takes a while (some vehicles are quicker than others) for the current draw to reach steady state and stabilize.  Most vehicles take <2 minutes.  However, the way you disconnected the battery, then completed the circuit again with the ammeter will eliminate any benefit of waiting for it to stabilize before disconnecting the battery.  You simply need to wait after reconnecting the ammeter for it to stabilize.
Good job - you share a lot of great tips on diagnosis.

replies.text: Whole reason I was watching this video to make sure I was reading milliamps right and he shows me wrong lol.
50ma draw is to high.
Thank you. I saw that and thought I was crazy for a minute when he kept saying 25 milliamps LOL
Thanks for this. When you say keeping the leads in place for a minute or two wouldn't that damage the leads?
@njuham  250mA is not nearly high enough current to damage test leads.  Fyi, if current was exceeding the capacity of a lead, it would melt the insulation in mere seconds.

The only thing I would add is adding a fuse to one of the test leads rated lower than the fuse in the multimeter will help save trying to find the hard to replace fuse in your meter when the draw is higher than you expected, or you aren’t so smooth disconnecting the battery terminal and everything wakes up through your meter.

Agreed 👍 . the first thing I would do is check inside the vehicle to see if there's any accessories that are still plugged into an auxiliary power outlet ....ie, a phone charger

Which is why you then start testing circuits starting with accessories and lights. You can also research if there are any common issues for your vehicle like GM half ton chassis having failures of the trailer light block fuse

@[PLATE REDACTED] Cal-Van makes a slick tool called "AmpHound" that does this for you. You punch in what fuse size/rate you're looking at, put the probes on the test ports, and it tells you how much amperage is running through that fuse.

I love mine, can do a whole fuse panel in about 2 minutes.

Dont pull fuses.
Some modules will reset once they see voltage again and enter an active phase.
Do as @[PLATE REDACTED] said.
Measure voltage drop across the fuse.
To do this, set multimeter to mV setting and put the leads to the metal probe points on the tops of fuses.
You then look at the chart for a given rating
As a 5A fuse will drop more voltage drop than a 20A one even for the same current draw.

Why pull fuses? Every 2 prong auto style fuse [PLATE REDACTED] terminals on the top of the plastic body of the fuse. Just set ur meter and check for voltage on both sides of the fuse via the top terminals.

While doing my studies with BYD, I was given a sheet with parasitic draw rates, read as millivolt readings across the nodes of specific amperage fuses (eg. a draw of 0.5A across a 10A fuse would read ≈0.018V)! It's been very handy to have when I encounter these sorts of jobs, since I can just dig straight into the job without disconnecting anything and risking a reset

records.problem_title: How to charge 12v Car Battery
records.problem_description: Its seen as good practice to connect the black wire second, and to connect it to some bare metal part in the engine. When disconnecting, you disconnect that black wire first. How to Recharge Your Car Battery: Step-By-Step Step 1: Find your vehicle's battery and locate the positive and negative terminals. Most cars have their battery under the hood. The positive terminal is marked with a "+," and the negative terminal is marked with a "-." Sometimes the terminals are protected by plastic covers that need to be flipped out of the way. Other vehicles have their batteries in the trunk. In these instances, you'll often find a positive terminal to connect to. Use the car's under hood sheetmetal as the negative terminal. If you're struggling to find the battery and/or it's associated terminals, consult that handy owner's manual. Step 2: Verify your battery charger is unplugged and turned off. Before attaching the battery charger, it's important to verify no current is flowing through the charger before connecting it to the terminals on your vehicle. Unplugging the charger prevents sparks—which can be dangerous if your battery is leaking. Read the instructions that come with the battery charger, as each charger operates a little differently. Step 3: Attach the battery charger to your vehicle's battery terminals. Always start by attaching the charger's red clamp to the battery'

qa_threads.comment: Supposed you were to charge the battery via a UPS how would you set it up?

replies.text:
Hi! Yes, you can charge a car battery using a UPS, but only by plugging a regular 12V battery charger into the UPS’s AC outlet.

Never connect the battery directly to the UPS itself!

The UPS just works like a backup power source, giving your charger electricity just like a normal wall socket.

Just keep in mind:

Don’t use a charger that’s too powerful for the UPS — it might overload it.

UPSs are mainly for short-term backup, so this is best as a temporary or emergency fix.

So basically, the UPS powers the charger, but it doesn’t charge the battery directly.

Hope this helps 😊 — happy charging ⚡ and stay safe! 🔋
​@Carhow5thanks! I actually meant as a replacement to the UPS' battery!
@7HDF Ah, got it — thanks for clarifying! That’s a whole different setup 😊

qa_threads.comment: What about removing the cords? In the opposite order? Does it make a difference?

replies.text:
Hi!  Yes, it’s always best to connect and disconnect the cables in a certain order:

Connecting: first connect the red (+) cable to the battery’s positive terminal, then the black (–) to the negative.

Disconnecting: first remove the black (–) cable, then the red (+)

records.problem_title: Power windows not working in Kia Sportage - fuse location
records.problem_description: If the power windows in your Kia Sportage aren’t working, it doesn’t always mean there’s a serious electrical fault. In many cases, it’s just a blown fuse. In this video, I’ll show you the exact fuse locations for the power windows in a 4th generation Kia Sportage. I’ll go through all four fuses related to the power windows, including some surprising details—like how the driver’s automatic window uses a separate safety module fuse. This video shows you: • Where the interior fuse panel is located. • Which fuse controls which window. • The difference between LH, RH, SAFETY DRV, and SAFETY PASS fuses. • How to visually inspect and test fuses with a test light. Before replacing window switches or tearing into the door panel, make sure to check these fuses first! #KiaSportage #PowerWindows #Kia Viewer Problem Reports: In my Kia Sportage 4th Gen, the passenger window works perfectly fine from the passenger-side switch—it goes both up and down. From the master switch on the driver’s side, it also goes down, but it doesn’t go up. What do you think could be the issue? Is it likely just the master switch, or could it be something else?

records.problem_title: Clicking or knocking noise after turning off the engine in Kia Sportage
records.problem_description: In this video, I discuss the mysterious clicking or knocking noise that I hear when turning off the engine in my Kia Sportage. After noticing this sound began around 3,000 kilometers into owning the car, I took it to a Kia dealership where they identified the source as the throttle body. According to them, this noise is normal and common in many Kia vehicles. However, the sound wasn’t there when I first bought the car, raising questions about its consistency. Check out my video on how to clean the throttle body: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uUEpS7aTTdc To see if I could resolve the noise, I decided to clean the throttle body. Watch until the end to see if cleaning it helped, and share your experience if you’re a Kia Sportage owner who has encountered this issue! #KiaSportage #EngineNoise #ThrottleBody #ClickingNoise #KiaOwners #Kia Viewer Problem Reports: Very helpful! I have a 2018 KIa Soul with 40,000 miles it just started this exact same issue. Thanks so much! | I had this noise develop at 5200 miles on [PLATE REDACTED] Kia Seltos SX when ever I shut my car off. I was able to isolate at least some of the noise is coming from the throttle body and I could easily hear it while sitting in my car with the hood closed. I could not definitively find a cause although many people say they have this issue start at some point for them as well.. After looking into this for several days I decided to accept it as the new norm. Then my Daughter drove the car to Great Adventure which is about an hour of highway driving each way, and she reached speeds of 80 mph per my speed tracking software. When she returned the problem had magically disappeared, and has not returned for the entire week. Since we typically drive the care short distances and never get up to highway speed I suspect I was having some carbon build up on the throttle body or somewhere and the high speed for an extended period burned it all off. If it ever comes back I will do this again. I believe it is called an Italian Tune-up | Now the exact same noise just appeared from my Kia K5 and I thought it was the engine issue…I searched on YT and found your video and realized I am not alone…Ha Ha..I dont really like that noise and want to know what the issue is so I just booked an appointment at Kia Service here in Myanmar…Thanks for your video and I will share my experience when I come back from Kia Service

Left unchecked, coolant leaks can cause overheating, engine damage, and even leave you stranded. 😬 That’s why catching and fixing them early is crucial! 🔧 **The Fix:** - Replaced the worn heater core hoses to restore heating for the sleeper area. - Installed a new, heavy-duty radiator coolant hose to handle the pressure and keep the system sealed. - Topped off and tested the cooling system to ensure it’s road-ready. 💡 **Pro Tip:** Regularly inspect your coolant hoses for cracks, wear, or loose clamps. records.problem_title: Pakistan Workshop Restores HONDA CITY After SERIOUS ACCIDENT - Pakistan Repair - @accidentmaster
records.problem_description: This video shows the restoration process of a badly damaged Honda City in a Pakistani workshop. Skilled Pakistani workers begin the repair by removing the doors, windows, lights, front panel, rear panel, and roof sections to gain access to the body structure. records.problem_title: Torque Converter – The Bane of Mechanics #TorqueTek
records.problem_description: Torque Converter – The Bane of Mechanics The torque converter is a mechanic’s nightmare. To repair it, the entire transmission must be removed, because the TC sits between the engine and the gearbox. Its housing is usually welded shut, so opening it requires cutting, grinding, and welding it back — not every workshop has the tools and experience for that. Most repairs involve replacing the lock-up clutch friction plates , bearing and seals. If the pump/turbine blade sealing or fluid pressure is not carefully checked, it’s easy to miss a fault — and the unit could fail again just a few days after reassembly. #TorqueTek #Shorts #Machines #automobile #Torque #horsepower

records.problem_title: Get rid of tremors today | Expert Advice #health #healthylifestyle
records.problem_description: Tremors are involuntary, rhythmic muscle contractions leading to shaking movements in one or more parts of the body. They can occur in the hands, arms, head, face, voice, trunk, or legs and can vary in intensity. Tremors can be caused by a range of conditions or factors, including: 1. Essential tremor: The most common type, often hereditary, typically affecting the hands and arms, especially when performing tasks like writing or holding objects. 2. Parkinson’s disease: A neurological condition that often causes resting tremors, particularly in the hands. 3. Multiple sclerosis (MS): Can cause tremors due to nerve damage in the brain or spinal cord. 4. Hyperthyroidism: An overactive thyroid can lead to fine hand tremors. 5. Medications: Some drugs, like those used for asthma or psychiatric conditions, can induce tremors as a side effect. 6. Anxiety or stress: Tremors can sometimes occur during heightened emotional states. 7. Caffeine: Excessive intake can cause temporary tremors. 8. Alcohol withdrawal: Tremors can be a symptom of alcohol withdrawal. If you’re concerned about tremors, seeking medical advice for an accurate diagnosis and potential treatments is essential, as some types can be managed with medications, physical therapy, or lifestyle changes. replies.text:
Rattles too, but sound is vibrations. Stopping the sheet metal from vibrating helps to stop the transfer of outside noises coming into the cabin. But its a case of diminishing returns. About 2 layers of medium thickness on the areas specifically that have a "drum" effect when you knock on it is where most should stop. 

The next step after should be the foam mats, which helps to reduce noise coming from in the cabin itself by absorbing the sound bouncing around inside the cabin, but its not very effective at reducing outside sounds, just catching the sounds that already made it inside and reducing it.

The mass loaded vinyl is best for reducing the sound of the loudest things at the source specifically such as your engine and exhaust by only putting it in the trunk or firewall, but the rest of the cabin wont make a big enough difference to be worth adding it because the butyl rubber mats will have already reduced the sound by around 80-ish % coming from those spots. but you can still do it for a small gain in benefit, maybe [PLATE REDACTED]% extra and in some cases like 10% if you have a very large cabin.

records.problem_title: Repairing a Leaking Plastic Radiator
records.problem_description: If your car radiator has a small leak, you may be wondering if it is possible to repair a plastic radiator and fix a radiator leak. Afterall, there is high-pressure, high-temperature coolant in the radiator tank. You may ask yourself, "How can a radiator epoxy adhesive possibly hold up under those conditions?" The answer is that it probably can't. It may fix the radiator leak temporarily, but over time, the radiator adhesive will, more than likely, come off. If you take your car to a radiator repair shop to repair a leaking radiator, you will often find that they will repair metal radiator tanks but NOT repair plastic radiator tanks. Instead, the radiator repair shop will probably try to sell you a replacement radiator. The replacement radiator cost can be very high compared to just repairing something so minor and easily repairable. Radiator tank repairs are not difficult at all. Just keep in mind a few things when you are repairing a cracked plastic radiator tank. First, the repair has to withstand high operating temperatures (200°F [PLATE REDACTED]°C and up). Second, the repair has to contain hot, pressurized coolant, making it immediately obvious when your weld is less-than-perfect. Because of the harsh operating conditions, the radiator tanks are made from glass-reinforced nylon, a plastic that features a high-softening point. records.problem_title: Losing Coolant? Maybe not...
records.problem_description: WARNING - Some coolant canisters are pressurized, read the cap and user manual before opening. Looking at how the expansion or overflow tank and radiator work on your car and why you may think you might be losing coolant and common things to look for before taking your car to the dealer. Viewer Problem Reports: "If you see the coolant leaking it could be a sign of a leak"
owner_problem_questions: "If you see the coolant leaking it could be a sign of a leak"
mechanic_and_community_solutions: Some coolant tanks are pressurized, please read your user manual before opening and check for warnings on the cap! | ​@okongtekuif your rad cap is good. This means you have air entering the system.you may have a leaking hose (rev engine to 2500 rpm when hot check hose for leak or pressurise cold engine)may also be the system was not properly bleed if you have just had some work done. | On my coolant expansion tank it says “cold fill level” meaning coolant level should be between min and max when engine is cold, you always check on the cold engine also, leads me to believe it should not go below min when cold, it’s potentially indicating a leak
Some coolant tanks are pressurized, please read your user manual before opening and check for warnings on the cap!

​@okongtekuif your rad cap is good. This means you have air entering the system.you may have a leaking hose (rev engine to 2500 rpm when hot check hose for leak or pressurise cold engine)may also be the system was not properly bleed if you have just had some work done.

On my coolant expansion tank it says “cold fill level” meaning coolant level should be between min and max when engine is cold, you always check on the cold engine also, leads me to believe it should not go below min when cold, it’s potentially indicating a leak
This makes me feel so much better, I will check the radiator, I have been worried because my expansion tank is always at the low when cold. I kept filling it up as didn't know any better.

Check your radiator cap and replace if its old. The sealing rubber is probably worn out. New cap and everything returns to normal operation if there are no leaks or coolant entering into the combustion...

Thank you. Good advice and explanation for a system many may misunderstand.

I would add that technically it's ok if the overflow is low/empty as long as the radiator is full. However it's not the optimal way to keep the car running. If you check the Subaru manual, it will tell you to check the overflow tank level when the car is cold (fully cooled down over night ideally). If the coolant level is at or below the low mark, fill it with coolant until you reach the full mark. That overflow tank serves two functions. It is an overflow tank and a gauge. When the car is warmed up, coolant will expand and flow into the overflow tank. When the car cools down, the coolant will contract and the radiator will suck back in coolant from the overflow tank. If the overflow is empty, it's sucking air in instead of coolant as designed. It's not the end of the world, but not ideal either. The tank also allows you to take a quick look under the hood and see if you're losing coolant or not without popping the radiotor cap off every time. It's only accurate when completely cold. When it's warm, it will go above the full mark, but that's fine. It's not going to spill out. If it does spill out, it means you were doing track days. 
If your tank is that empty and you fill it to the full mark when it's cold, don't be surprised if the coolant level drops after a few drive cycles. Keep topping it up while it's stone cold. Run the heat in the cabin to help get any air trapped in the system out. It'll eventually settle to the full mark where it should be when stone cold. If you're radiator is full to the top and after about 2-4 top ups of the overflow it's still going low, you may have a problem.

Nice. Great. Fantastic explanation. Just recently got into doing repairs on [PLATE REDACTED] Subaru Crosstrek with worries on my coolant. Luckily, I decided to check this channel before making any firm decisions and, as always, I found a video relating to my issue. Thank you Kurt of Trades for all your hard work!

thank you for the video. My car once lost water and got heated. I ve got white smoke from the exhaust. i got to the technician who filled it up with fluid checked out for leaks (didnt find any) also replaced the radiator cap. So he got suspicious of the fluids going into the engine.  I drived the car for about 2 weeks. Everything looked normal driving was like nothing ever happened no heating and radiator properly full. The only problem was that the overflow tank used to get lower as much as the car was moving. That happened little by little needing lets say a distance of 100kms until it got at low level. When i filled up it got low again after 100kms. So finally i got my car for engine service. The check up showed destroyed gasket and cylinders. We replaced the engine cylinders and pistons for a full reconditioning and replaced the overflow tank and radiator as well. After that car was again driving and moving fine and radiator is always full. But the overflow tank still loses coolant at a same pace as before. That is a 5 months situation with me filling up the tank with water or coolant. Although technican told me that i don't have to do so. I am afraid of loosing coolant from the tank and then from the radiator during a trip and then get any serious damage again. We did a double check for coolant leak and didnt find any. Replaced again the cap.Technician insists there is no fluid pulled back in engine. But what does  this coolant getting lower mean? Could that be the reason for the heating at first place? So i may run on same problems again? Or an empty overflow tank is just a  normal situation as long radiator is full? Unfortunately never checked how overflow tank functioned before the heating. So it is like a mistery..

I dont have a youtube channel, but I do know a trick I tried once and it worked, if the car is not starting due to low battery,
1. Remove the negative terminal from the battery
2. Get another person to start from the inside and ask him to place the key in ignition.
3. Take the negative wire and touch and take the wire consecutively from the terminal, you will sense it will try to start.
4. At a particular time it would ignited and have almost started,at that time do not remove the terminal. and place it to the terminal.
This process also needs two people but you dont need to push the vehicle and waste energy, you just need the correct spanner to remove the terminal wire.
Make sure you drive for few kilometers after starting for the alternator to recharge the battery.
If you see this comment, try it out it will work..

qa_threads.comment:
NOTE: DO NOT use a pressure washer while cleaning your engine bay. Engine bay is designed in a way, so that it can be cleanable but pressured water can enter into electrical connectors and small wire holes which can damage the electrical system over time and cause rust.
Always use a mild gardening water pipe which is used to water plants, its much safer and it doesnt let water enter into tiny spaces such as the fusebox, temperature sensors or abs wires.
After cleaning the engine bay with gardening water pipe, use a leaf blower(if possible) or a towel to wipe the remaining water. 
Remember always remove the undertray from under the engine bay, that way the water isnt stuck in the engine bay. And always AVOID using pressure washer shown in the video.
(You dont need to cover the battery wires but if you feel unsafe you can its your choice)
